parts.title: Joining a swimming course
parts.setting: A student phones a leisure centre to ask about swimming lessons for beginners.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a student phoning a leisure centre to ask about swimming lessons.
RECEPTIONIST: Good morning, Riverside Leisure Centre. How can I help you?
STUDENT: Good morning. My name is Ana Sharma. I am a first-year student at the university, and I would like to join a swimming course for beginners.
RECEPTIONIST: Of course, Ana. We run beginner courses on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, and also on Saturday mornings.
STUDENT: Saturday morning would suit me best. What time does it start?
RECEPTIONIST: The Saturday class starts at half past nine and lasts for one hour.
STUDENT: That sounds good. How long does the whole course last?
RECEPTIONIST: It runs for eight weeks, and there is a short break in the middle for the public holiday weekend.
STUDENT: And how much does it cost?
RECEPTIONIST: The full course is ninety pounds, but students get a discount, so you would pay sixty-five pounds.
STUDENT: That is reasonable. Do I need to bring anything with me?
RECEPTIONIST: Just a swimming costume, a towel, and a pair of goggles if you have them. We provide swimming caps and all the other equipment.
STUDENT: I do not have goggles yet. Can I buy them at the centre?
RECEPTIONIST: Yes, we sell them at reception for eight pounds.
STUDENT: Good. Is there a test before I start, to check my level?
RECEPTIONIST: No test, but the instructor will watch you swim a short distance in the first lesson, just to place you in the right group.
STUDENT: I can swim a little, but I cannot do a proper front crawl yet.
RECEPTIONIST: That is fine. Most beginners are in the same position. The course starts with breathing and floating, then moves on to the basic strokes.
STUDENT: One more thing — is there somewhere to leave my bag while I swim?
RECEPTIONIST: Yes, there are lockers beside the pool. You need a one-pound coin, which you get back afterwards.
STUDENT: How do I book a place?
RECEPTIONIST: You can book online, or I can take your details now and reserve a place for you.
STUDENT: Please reserve a place for me now. My email is ana.sharma@studentmail.com.
RECEPTIONIST: Thank you. I will send you a confirmation email today, and you need to pay by Friday the twentieth of September.
STUDENT: Friday the twentieth — I will make a note of that. Where is the centre, exactly?
RECEPTIONIST: We are on Mill Road, next to the bus station. The nearest bus stop is just outside the main entrance.
STUDENT: Perfect. Thank you very much for your help.
RECEPTIONIST: You are welcome, Ana. We look forward to seeing you on Saturday.

parts.title: A guided walk around Riverside Park
parts.setting: A volunteer welcomes visitors to a guided walk around a riverside park.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a volunteer welcoming visitors to a guided walk around a riverside park.
GUIDE: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Riverside Park. My name is Tom Baker, and I will be your guide for the next hour and a half.
GUIDE: The park was opened in 1924, when the land was given to the town by the Hartley family, who owned the large house you can see across the river.
GUIDE: Before we start, let me tell you a little about the route. We will walk along the river path first, then cross the old stone bridge and come back through the woodland garden.
GUIDE: The whole walk is about two kilometres, and the paths are flat, so it should be comfortable for everyone, including people with pushchairs.
GUIDE: Our first stop is the boathouse, which was built in 1890. In the past, boats carried goods up and down the river, but today the boathouse is used by the local rowing club.
GUIDE: If you look across the water, you can see the heronry. About forty grey herons nest there every spring, and if we are lucky, we may see one fishing in the shallow water near the bank.
GUIDE: Further along the path, we will pass the rose garden. It has more than two hundred varieties of roses, and the best time to see them is in June, when they are all in flower.
GUIDE: The park is also home to a small cafe, the Riverside Cafe, which is open every day from nine in the morning until five in the afternoon. It serves hot drinks, sandwiches, and homemade cakes.
GUIDE: Now, a few practical points. There are toilets near the main entrance and also beside the cafe. Dogs are welcome in the park, but they must be kept on a lead near the children's playground.
GUIDE: The playground was rebuilt last year, and it now has a climbing frame, swings, and a sandpit for younger children.
GUIDE: Each summer, the park hosts a music festival. This year, the festival takes place on the third weekend of July, and entry is free, although visitors are asked to make a small donation.
GUIDE: Finally, if you enjoy today's walk, the Friends of Riverside Park meet on the first Saturday of every month to help with planting and litter picking. New members are always welcome.
GUIDE: Right, let us begin. Please follow me down to the river path, and do watch your step on the wooden bridge — it can be slippery after rain.

parts.title: Planning a presentation on renewable energy
parts.setting: Two students discuss their group presentation with their tutor.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing a group presentation with their tutor.
TUTOR: Good afternoon, Maya and Daniel. How is your group presentation coming along?
MAYA: It is going well, Dr Evans. We have decided to focus on renewable energy in small towns, and Daniel has found some very useful data.
DANIEL: Yes, I looked at three towns in the north of England that now get most of their electricity from wind and solar power.
TUTOR: That sounds like a good angle. How long is the presentation?
MAYA: Twenty minutes, plus five minutes for questions from the class.
TUTOR: And how have you divided the work between you?
DANIEL: I will introduce the topic and explain how wind turbines work. Maya will talk about solar power and the costs, and then we will present our conclusions together.
MAYA: We have also made a short video of an interview with the manager of a wind farm near Leeds. We would like to show a two-minute clip from it.
TUTOR: That could work well, but make sure the clip adds something new. Do not just repeat what you have already said.
DANIEL: Good point. The manager talks about the problems they faced when the wind farm was built, which we have not covered in the main talk.
TUTOR: Excellent. What about your sources? Have you used enough academic material?
MAYA: We have used two journal articles and a government report from last year. I was worried that might not be enough.
TUTOR: Three good sources are fine for a twenty-minute talk, but make sure you list them all on your final slide.
DANIEL: We also wanted to include a graph showing how electricity prices have changed over the last ten years. Is that a good idea?
TUTOR: Yes, a clear graph is always helpful, but keep it simple — no more than three lines on one graph.
MAYA: When is the deadline for the slides?
TUTOR: You need to send me the slides by Thursday evening, so I can check them before your presentation on Monday morning.
DANIEL: Monday morning — that is the ninth of June, is it not?
TUTOR: Yes, the ninth of June, at ten o'clock, in Room 4 of the Science Building.
MAYA: One more question. Should we give the class a handout?
TUTOR: A one-page summary would be useful, but do not print the whole presentation. Just the main points and your three sources.
DANIEL: Thanks, Dr Evans. We will send you the slides on Thursday.
TUTOR: Good. I am looking forward to it.

parts.title: Sleep and memory
parts.setting: A university lecturer gives a talk about how sleep affects memory.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about sleep and memory.
LECTURER: Good morning. Today I want to talk about something that affects every student in this room: the link between sleep and memory.
LECTURER: Most of us think of sleep as a time when the brain switches off. In fact, the brain is extremely busy while we sleep, and one of its most important jobs is to organise what we have learned during the day.
LECTURER: Sleep has two main stages that matter for memory. The first is deep sleep, which happens mostly in the first half of the night. During deep sleep, the brain moves new facts — like the names and dates you studied — from short-term storage into long-term memory.
LECTURER: The second stage is REM sleep, which stands for rapid eye movement sleep. This happens mostly in the second half of the night, and it seems to be important for skills and for emotional memories.
LECTURER: A famous experiment at Harvard University showed this very clearly. Two groups of students were taught a new skill in the evening. One group slept normally, while the other group stayed awake all night. The next morning, the group that had slept performed twenty per cent better on the test.
LECTURER: So what does this mean for students? First, it means that staying up all night before an exam is usually a bad idea. You may feel that you have studied more, but without sleep, much of that information will not be stored properly.
LECTURER: Second, short naps can help. A nap of twenty to thirty minutes in the afternoon can improve your ability to remember new words, although a nap longer than an hour can leave you feeling sleepy.
LECTURER: Third, regular sleep matters more than one good night. Students who sleep seven to eight hours every night remember more over a whole term than students whose sleep changes a lot from night to night.
LECTURER: Finally, what you do before bed matters too. Reading your notes for fifteen minutes in the evening, and then going to sleep, is more effective than reading the same notes for an hour in the morning.
LECTURER: To sum up, sleep is not wasted time. It is part of learning itself. If you want to remember what you study, protect your sleep as carefully as you protect your study time.

parts.title: Renting a flat near the university
parts.setting: A student phones a letting agent about a flat near the university.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a student phoning a letting agent about a flat.
AGENT: Good afternoon, City Lets. This is James speaking. How can I help?
STUDENT: Hello, my name is Ben Carter. I am looking for a one-bedroom flat near the university, and I saw your advertisement for a flat on Oak Street.
AGENT: Yes, the Oak Street flat is still available. It is on the second floor, and it is about a ten-minute walk from the main campus.
STUDENT: That sounds ideal. How much is the rent?
AGENT: The rent is five hundred and fifty pounds a month, and that includes water and heating, but not electricity.
STUDENT: Is there a deposit?
AGENT: Yes, the deposit is one month's rent, and you will get it back at the end of the tenancy if there is no damage to the flat.
STUDENT: When could I move in?
AGENT: The flat is available from the first of October. The current tenant is moving out at the end of September.
STUDENT: Could I come and see the flat this week?
AGENT: Of course. I can show you round on Wednesday afternoon at three o'clock, or on Thursday morning at eleven.
STUDENT: Wednesday at three would be perfect. What is the flat like inside?
AGENT: It is quite small but very bright. There is a living room with a sofa and a small dining table, a separate kitchen, and a bathroom with a shower. There is no bath, I am afraid.
STUDENT: Is there internet in the flat?
AGENT: Not yet, but the previous tenant had broadband, so the connection is already there. You would just need to choose a provider.
STUDENT: And is there any parking?
AGENT: There is no private parking, but you can park on the street with a resident's permit, which costs forty pounds a year from the council.
STUDENT: I do not have a car, so that does not matter. Is the area quiet at night?
AGENT: Yes, Oak Street is a quiet residential street, and most of the neighbours are families and postgraduate students.
STUDENT: That sounds good. Can I bring a friend to the viewing on Wednesday?
AGENT: Certainly. Just meet me outside the main entrance at three o'clock, and please bring some photo identification with you.
STUDENT: I will bring my passport. Thank you very much.
AGENT: You are welcome, Ben. I will see you on Wednesday.

parts.title: A tour of the university botanical garden
parts.setting: A guide introduces visitors to a university botanical garden.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a guide introducing visitors to a botanical garden.
GUIDE: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the university botanical garden. My name is Dr Helen Wright, and I manage the garden's education programme.
GUIDE: The garden covers twelve hectares, and it is home to more than eight thousand different kinds of plants, from tiny alpine flowers to trees that are over two hundred years old.
GUIDE: The garden was founded in 1831 as a place where medical students could learn about plants used in medicine. Today, it is used for teaching, research, and by the public, who are welcome to visit free of charge.
GUIDE: We will begin our tour in the glasshouses, where the temperature is kept at twenty-five degrees all year round. Inside, you will see plants from tropical rainforests, including orchids, palms, and a banana tree that produces fruit every summer.
GUIDE: From there, we will walk to the rock garden, which was built in 1935 from stone brought from the mountains of Wales. The small plants that grow there come from high places all over the world, where the summers are short and the winters are very cold.
GUIDE: Next, we will visit the herb garden. Many of the herbs here have been used as medicines for hundreds of years. For example, the leaves of the foxglove plant were once used to treat heart problems, and they are still the source of an important modern drug.
GUIDE: After the herb garden, we will stop at the lake, where you can see water lilies and a family of ducks that has lived here for many years. Please do not feed the ducks, as bread can make them ill.
GUIDE: The garden is open every day from ten in the morning until six in the evening, except on Christmas Day. The best time to visit is in May, when the spring flowers are at their best and the trees are full of blossom.
GUIDE: Before we start, let me mention the garden shop, which sells seeds, books, and plants grown here in the garden. All the money from the shop goes back into looking after the garden.
GUIDE: Finally, if you would like to learn more, we run a short course on gardening for beginners every Saturday morning in the autumn. The course costs thirty pounds for six weeks, and you can sign up at the visitor centre.
GUIDE: Now, if everyone is ready, please follow me into the first glasshouse, and mind the step as you go in — it is a little higher than it looks.

parts.title: Discussing a field trip report on river water
parts.setting: Two students discuss their field trip report on river water quality with their tutor.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear two students discussing a field trip report with their tutor.
TUTOR: Hello, Sara and Tom. Let us talk about your field trip report on the River Avon. How did the trip go?
SARA: It went very well, Dr Green. We visited three sites along the river and took water samples at each one.
TOM: The first site was near the town centre, the second was next to a farm, and the third was in the nature reserve, about five kilometres downstream.
TUTOR: Good. And what did your results show?
SARA: The water at the nature reserve was the cleanest. It had the lowest level of nitrates and the highest level of oxygen, which is a good sign for fish.
TOM: The site next to the farm had the worst results. The nitrate level there was three times higher than at the nature reserve, probably because of fertiliser washing off the fields.
TUTOR: That is an important finding. Did you check your results against the official standards?
SARA: Yes, we compared them with the Environment Agency's guidelines. The farm site was above the safe limit for nitrates, but the other two sites were within the limit.
TUTOR: What about the samples from the town centre?
TOM: They were in the middle. The oxygen level was lower than at the nature reserve, but the water was still safe for most fish species.
TUTOR: How are you going to present these results in your report?
SARA: We are going to use a table for the main numbers, and a bar chart to show the nitrate levels at the three sites.
TUTOR: A bar chart is a good choice. Make sure you label both axes clearly, and include the units.
TOM: We also took photographs at each site. Should we include them in the report?
TUTOR: Yes, two or three photographs would be helpful, especially if they show the land use around each site. But do not include too many.
SARA: When is the report due?
TUTOR: The deadline is Friday the fourteenth of November, and you should submit it through the online system, not by email.
TOM: We will need to write about two thousand words. Is that right?
TUTOR: Yes, two thousand words, not including the table and the references. And please include a short conclusion with one clear recommendation.
SARA: Our recommendation is that farmers should leave a ten-metre strip of grass between their fields and the river. That would reduce the fertiliser reaching the water.
TUTOR: That is a sensible recommendation. Well done, both of you. I will look forward to reading the report.

parts.title: Honeybees and pollination
parts.setting: A university lecturer gives a talk about honeybees and their role in farming.
parts.transcript:
NARRATOR: You will hear a lecture about honeybees and pollination.
LECTURER: Good afternoon. In today's lecture, I want to look at one of the most important animals in agriculture: the honeybee.
LECTURER: Most people know that bees make honey, but their real value lies in pollination. When a bee visits a flower to collect nectar, pollen sticks to its body, and when the bee moves to the next flower, some of that pollen is left behind. This allows the plant to produce seeds and fruit.
LECTURER: Around three quarters of the world's food crops depend on pollinators to some extent. Crops such as apples, almonds, and coffee all produce much smaller harvests without bees.
LECTURER: Unfortunately, honeybee numbers have been falling in many countries. In the United States, for example, beekeepers have lost about forty per cent of their colonies in some recent winters.
LECTURER: There are several reasons for this decline. The first is the loss of habitat. As more land is used for housing and for large fields of a single crop, bees have fewer wild flowers to feed on.
LECTURER: The second reason is pesticides. Some chemicals used to protect crops from insects can also harm bees, damaging their ability to find their way back to the hive.
LECTURER: The third reason is disease. A tiny mite called Varroa attacks young bees and spreads viruses through the colony. Beekeepers now have to treat their hives regularly to keep this mite under control.
LECTURER: What can be done? Farmers can help by planting strips of wild flowers along the edges of their fields. Studies have shown that these flower strips can increase the number of wild bees in an area by up to fifty per cent.
LECTURER: Gardeners can help too, by growing plants that flower at different times of the year, so that bees always have food. Even a small balcony with a few pots can make a difference.
LECTURER: Finally, scientists are working on new ways to protect bees, including breeding bees that are more resistant to the Varroa mite and developing safer pesticides.
LECTURER: To conclude, bees are not just honey producers. They are essential workers in our food system, and protecting them is one of the simplest ways to protect our food supply.
